lead: A switched-mode power supply (SMPS) does not burn off excess voltage as heat. It switches the input on and off thousands of times a second, stores energy in an inductor or capacitor, and releases it to the load at the wanted voltage. Feedback adjusts the on-time fraction, called duty cycle, to hold the output steady. Phone chargers, laptop adapters, TV sets and UPI payment terminals all use an SMPS. Its efficiency often exceeds 85 percent, which is why it replaced bulky linear supplies in most mains-powered equipment.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 on IC regulators, and the energy-storage idea for an inductor (½Li²) and capacitor (½Cv²).

sections.h3: The switch replaces the pass transistor

blocks.text: The problem with linear regulators. A series regulator in Chapter 1.5 holds the output by dropping the extra voltage across a pass transistor. If Vin = 24 V and Vout = 9.6 V at 1 A, the transistor burns (24 − 9.6) × 1 = 14.4 W as heat. The best possible efficiency is Vout/Vin = 40 percent.

A switched-mode power supply, or SMPS, avoids that heat. It uses a transistor as a switch that is either fully on (low voltage across it) or fully off (no current). In both states the power wasted in the switch is small. The switch chops the input into pulses. An inductor and capacitor store the pulse energy and smooth it into steady DC. Some syllabi call these circuits switching regulators.

blocks.where: D is duty cycle (0 to 1); Ton is on-time in seconds; T is switching period in seconds; fsw = 1/T is switching frequency in hertz.

blocks.text: A pulse-width modulator (PWM) compares a sample of Vout with a reference and sets D. If Vout falls, D rises and more energy moves to the output.
Three topologies cover most needs. All formulas assume continuous conduction mode (CCM): the inductor current never reaches zero during a cycle.

Buck (step-down): Vout = D Vin. Here Vout and Vin are in volts and D is dimensionless. The switch connects Vin to the inductor for D T. The freewheeling diode carries inductor current for the rest. With Vin = 24 V and D = 0.4, Vout = 0.4 × 24 = 9.6 V.

Boost (step-up): Vout = Vin / (1 − D). The inductor is first connected across Vin to store energy; then the switch opens and the inductor pushes current through a diode into the output capacitor. With Vin = 12 V and D = 0.5, Vout = 12/(1 − 0.5) = 24 V. The output is always greater than Vin.
Buck-boost (inverting): Vout = −Vin × D/(1 − D). The magnitude can be lower or higher than Vin; the sign reverses. Many isolated supplies use a transformer instead, which also gives isolation.

blocks.where: ΔIL is peak-to-peak inductor current in amperes; Vin and Vout are in volts; D is dimensionless; T is in seconds; L is inductance in henries. The off-time expression Vout (1 − D) T / L gives the same ripple, because the average inductor voltage over one cycle is zero.

blocks.text: Component roles: the inductor limits current change and stores ½ L i²; the output capacitor stores ½ C v² and holds Vout between pulses. Higher fsw allows smaller L and C.

Losses and efficiency. Conduction loss in the switch is approximately I² Rds(on) D, where I is switch current in amperes and Rds(on) is the MOSFET on-resistance in ohms. Switching loss occurs while the switch passes through the linear region: roughly ½ Vin I (tr + tf) fsw, where tr and tf are rise and fall times in seconds. At high fsw this term grows, so there is a practical limit around a few hundred kilohertz for silicon MOSFETs.

The freewheeling diode in a buck converter drops about 0.4 to 0.7 V. At Vout = 1.2 V this diode loss can dominate. Synchronous rectification replaces the diode with a MOSFET that is switched on when the diode would conduct. Its drop is I Rds(on), often 50 mV or less, so efficiency rises, especially at low output voltages.

blocks.where: ΔVout is peak-to-peak output ripple in volts; ΔIL is inductor ripple in amperes; fsw is in hertz; C is output capacitance in farads. This ignores capacitor ESR; real ripple has an extra term ΔIL × ESR.

blocks.text: Control-loop compensation — setting the error amplifier's gain and phase so the loop does not oscillate — is left to advanced power electronics.

examples.question: A buck converter has Vin = 24 V, duty cycle D = 0.4, switching frequency fsw = 100 kHz and inductor L = 100 µH. Find the ideal output voltage and the inductor current ripple in continuous conduction.
steps: Ideal output Vout = D Vin = 0.4 × 24 = 9.6 V.
On-time Ton = D T = 0.4 × 10 µs = 4 µs.
Voltage across the inductor during on-time = Vin − Vout = 24 − 9.6 = 14.4 V.
Check with off-time: Vout (1 − D) T / L = 9.6 × 0.6 × 10 × 10⁻⁶ / (100 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.576 A. The two answers agree.
examples.answer: Ideal output voltage is 9.6 V and inductor current ripple is 0.576 A peak-to-peak.

traps: Swapping buck and boost formulas. Buck gives Vout = D Vin, less than Vin; boost gives Vin/(1 − D), more than Vin. Write the topology name before substituting.
Using D as 40 instead of 0.4 in a formula. Duty cycle is a fraction; multiply by 100 only when you report percent.
Treating the ideal formula as the real output. Diode drop, switch drop and losses lower the measured Vout; an unloaded converter may sit slightly high.
Applying the CCM ripple formula at light load. If the inductor current reaches zero, the converter is in DCM and the formula overestimates ripple.
Forgetting that the buck-boost output is inverted. The magnitude is D Vin/(1 − D); the minus sign matters in polarity and in feedback sensing.

quiz.q: Define duty cycle and write its formula.
quiz.a: Duty cycle is the fraction of the switching period for which the switch is on. D = Ton/T = Ton fsw, where Ton is on-time, T is period and fsw is switching frequency. D lies between 0 and 1.

quiz.q: Why can an SMPS be more efficient than a series linear regulator?
quiz.a: The switch is either off (no current) or on (small voltage), so it does not continuously dissipate (Vin − Vout)I. Energy is temporarily stored in L and C. The linear pass transistor always carries load current with the full difference voltage across it.

quiz.q: A boost converter has Vin = 12 V and D = 0.5 in CCM. Find Vout.
A buck converter has Vin = 20 V, D = 0.25, fsw = 200 kHz and L = 50 µH. Find Vout and the inductor current ripple in CCM.
A buck converter in CCM suddenly gets a heavier load. Describe what happens to Vout and how PWM restores it.
quiz.a: Vout dips because inductor current cannot change instantly. The error amplifier sees the fall and increases D. The switch on-time lengthens, average inductor current rises until it matches the new load, and Vout returns to the set value. Loop compensation sets the speed and stability of this recovery.

quiz.q: Why does raising fsw shrink L and C but hurt efficiency?
quiz.a: Inductor ripple ΔIL is proportional to 1/(fsw L), so smaller L gives the same ripple at higher fsw. Output ripple is proportional to 1/(fsw C), so C can also shrink. But switching loss is proportional to fsw, and gate-drive loss rises too.

quiz.q: What is synchronous rectification and where does it help most?
quiz.a: It replaces the freewheeling diode with a MOSFET switched on when the diode would conduct. The drop becomes I Rds(on) instead of a fixed diode voltage. It helps most at low output voltages, where a 0.5 V diode drop is a large fraction of Vout.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wide-bandgap switches such as GaN and SiC allow higher fsw with lower switching loss, shrinking magnetics further. Digital control loops and PMIC chips integrate the PWM, feedback and protection on one die. EMI and thermal design decide whether a good schematic becomes a reliable product. Search terms: synchronous buck, CCM versus DCM, GaN half-bridge, power management IC.
